To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the pigeon's NCL contains neurons that respond to stimuli that predict reward, respond to stimuli that do not predict reward, respond when reward is expected but not delivered and respond to instrumental behavior.
NCL neurons represent reward value, instrumental actions and action outcomes, and that they therefore provide signals useful in dynamically changing environments.
NCL neurons represent the reward value of stimuli, instrumental actions and action outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how animals learn to solve complex problems.
the neural basis of adaptive behavior in the pigeon.
the neural mechanisms underlying the ability of animals to learn to perform goal-directed behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NCL represents information useful for adaptive behavior.

the NCL neurons represent the reward value of a specific stimuli, instrumental action as well as action outcome, and therefore provides signals useful for adaptive behaviour in dynamically changing environments.
NCL neurons represent a variety of stimulus-response-outcome associations that are relevant for the regulation of goal-directed behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NCL provides the basis for the formation and maintenance of goal-directed behaviors.
the NCL is a multimodal associative structure that represents the reward value of stimuli, the value of instrumental actions, and the outcome of actions.
the NCL is a multimodal structure that is involved in stimulus-reward association and in the representation of stimulus-response-outcome contingencies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NCL neurons represent the stimulus, response, and outcome components of goal-directed behavior.
the NCL may be an important structure for goal-directed action control.
the NCL is involved in the representation of information that is useful for goal-directed action, and thus may be an avian analogue to prefrontal cortex.
